colourings.label: Overall capture score
colourings.note: Weighted combination of thirty-one country-by-country measures. Faded = less data.

colourings.label: Data available per country
colourings.note: How many of the scored measures cover each country. More measures means a more reliable score.

colourings.label: Evidence on file
colourings.note: How many verified studies and cases cover each country. Measures how much is documented, not how captured a country is.

colourings.label: Laws written or shaped by industry
colourings.note: Documented cases of companies drafting, copying into, or rewriting laws.

colourings.label: Policy follows the affluent
colourings.note: Gilens–Page style studies comparing what passes with what rich and poor citizens wanted.

colourings.label: Captured by other powers
colourings.note: Documented cases of foreign governments, armed groups, the military or the executive taking control of lawmaking.

colourings.label: Bribery or capture of the state
colourings.note: Court records and official inquiries into companies paying for laws, contracts or political access.

colourings.label: Top 1% share of income
colourings.note: Share of pre-tax national income received by the richest 1% (World Inequality Database, latest year, mostly 2024). Context for the score, not part of it by default.

colourings.label: Tobacco industry interference, 2025
colourings.note: Civil-society scoring of 100 governments, 0–100. Higher means more industry interference in health law.

colourings.label: Firms hit by bought laws, 1999
colourings.note: Share of firms in 22 post-Soviet and Eastern European economies whose business was significantly affected by purchased laws, decrees and rulings.

colourings.label: Which laws: Tax and financial secrecy (sector index)
colourings.note: Position 0 to 100 on financial secrecy and corporate tax haven scores (Tax Justice Network; average of the two where both exist) (100 = most captured).

colourings.label: Which laws: Health and tobacco (sector index)
colourings.note: Position 0 to 100 on tobacco industry interference (Global Tobacco Index) (100 = most captured).

colourings.label: Which laws: Environment, energy and resources (sector index)
colourings.note: Position 0 to 100 on oil, gas and mining governance (Natural Resource Governance Institute) (100 = most captured).

colourings.label: Which laws: Elections and political money (sector index)
colourings.note: Position 0 to 100 on legal bans on corporate and contractor donations (International IDEA) (100 = most captured).

colourings.label: Measure: Wealthy hold political power
colourings.note: Experts' rating of how far wealth turns into political power (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Legislators trade favors for money
colourings.note: Whether lawmakers take bribes, steer contracts to firms, or do favors for firms in return for later jobs (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Spending aimed at narrow interests
colourings.note: Whether the national budget mostly serves specific firms, sectors, groups or regions rather than the public as a whole (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Top 1% share of income (off by default)
colourings.note: Share of pre-tax national income going to the top 1% (World Inequality Database, mostly 2024). Measures the concentration of money that can buy influence, not influence itself, so it starts at weight 0.

colourings.label: Measure: Tobacco industry interference
colourings.note: Civil-society scoring of industry influence on health laws, 100 countries (2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Legislators use office for private gain
colourings.note: Surveys of households and legal experts on whether legislators abuse office for private gain (World Justice Project, 2024; 142 countries).

colourings.label: Measure: Regulation bent by improper influence
colourings.note: Whether government regulations are applied and enforced without improper influence, including from private interests (World Justice Project, 2024).

colourings.label: Measure: Public sees parliament as corrupt
colourings.note: How corrupt the public rates its parliament or legislature, 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely), in Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer (survey 2012–13; 105 countries). About corruption generally and over a decade old, so weighted half.

colourings.label: Measure: Public sees MPs as corrupt (Africa, 2019)
colourings.note: Share of people saying most or all members of parliament are corrupt, in Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer – Africa 2019, carried out by Afrobarometer in 35 countries. It asks the same kind of question as the 2013 parliament rating, so for African countries in both surveys the two partly overlap; weighted half.

colourings.label: Measure: Firms see laws shaped by legal donations and influence (2004)
colourings.note: Share of firms in the World Economic Forum's 2004 survey of business executives (104 countries) giving a satisfactory rating on how much legal political donations and undue political influence shape policy. From the World Bank's corporate ethics indices built by Daniel Kaufmann. Lower means more of this legal corruption. Old, and the source warns that small gaps between countries are not meaningful, so weighted low.

colourings.label: Measure: Laws built for financial secrecy
colourings.note: How much room a jurisdiction's laws give to hide money and ownership (Tax Justice Network, 2026; 141 jurisdictions).

colourings.label: Measure: Laws open to corporate money in politics
colourings.note: Whether the law bans corporate donations to parties and donations from government contractors (International IDEA; 178 countries).

colourings.label: Measure: Weak lobbying safeguards (Europe, 2015)
colourings.note: Transparency International's score of lobbying transparency, integrity and equal access in 19 European countries.

colourings.label: Measure: Criminal groups operating inside government
colourings.note: Experts' rating of how far state officials and agents take part in or enable organized crime (Global Organized Crime Index, 2025; 193 countries). Covers every illegal market, not only lawmaking, so weighted half.

colourings.label: Measure: Draft rules not opened to the public
colourings.note: Whether ministries ask the public to comment on draft regulations and report back on the comments, scored 0–2 with the World Bank's published rules (Global Indicators of Regulatory Governance, collected 2017–18; 186 countries). Measures openness of the process only: the World Bank notes it does not show whether comments change the rules, and industry also uses consultations.

colourings.label: Measure: Lawmaking and political money kept from view (Africa)
colourings.note: Average of three in-practice ratings: public access to legislative processes and documents, effective asset disclosure by senior officials including MPs, and parties' disclosure of private donations (Africa Integrity Indicators, 2025; 55 African countries and territories). Also one of the sources of the World Bank corruption measure, so weighted half.

colourings.label: Measure: Legislature can't check the executive
colourings.note: Whether the legislature and its agencies can question, investigate and oversee the executive (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Courts can't check the executive
colourings.note: Whether the executive respects the constitution and complies with court rulings, and courts act independently (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Military's hold on government
colourings.note: How far the military can appoint or remove the head of government (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Votes and policy traded for favors
colourings.note: How far politics runs on clientelism: votes and support exchanged for jobs, goods and favors (V-Dem, 2025).

colourings.label: Measure: Corruption, including state capture
colourings.note: World Bank aggregate of 30+ sources on public power used for private gain, including capture of the state by elites and private interests (2025). Partly built from V-Dem and WJP, so weighted lower.

colourings.label: Measure: Abuse of office goes unchecked
colourings.note: Bertelsmann experts' scores for anti-corruption policy and prosecution of office abuse in 137 developing and transition countries (BTI 2026).

colourings.label: Measure: Office abuse goes unchecked (OECD and EU)
colourings.note: Bertelsmann experts' score for how far public officeholders are prevented from abusing their positions, covering party-finance rules, asset declarations, conflict-of-interest rules and their enforcement (SGI 2024; 30 OECD and EU countries). The rich-country counterpart of the BTI measure.

colourings.label: Measure: Weak safeguards on lobbying and political money
colourings.note: OECD's check of four sets of criteria: rules on lobbying, conflict of interest and political finance, and whether lobbying transparency, party-finance oversight and conflict-of-interest checks on senior officials work in practice (Public Integrity Indicators; OECD members 2022, partner countries 2024; 55 countries with all four). Measures safeguards rather than influence.

colourings.label: Measure: Tax laws built for corporate tax abuse
colourings.note: How much room a jurisdiction's laws leave multinationals to avoid tax (Tax Justice Network, December 2025; 70 jurisdictions).

colourings.label: Measure: Oil, gas and mining governance
colourings.note: How well laws and practice govern resource licensing, taxes, state companies and revenues (Natural Resource Governance Institute, 2021; 18 countries).

colourings.label: Measure: Little public data on lobbying, money and assets
colourings.note: Whether governments publish usable data on lobbying, political finance, officials' assets and public consultations (Global Data Barometer, 2021; 108 countries). Measures openness about influence, not influence itself.

colourings.label: Measure: Stock market held by politicians' firms, 2001
colourings.note: Share of each country's stock-market value in firms whose owners or top officers sat in parliament or government (42 countries). Old, so weighted low.

colourings.label: Measure: Firms hit by bought votes and decrees, 2005
colourings.note: Average rating by firms (0 = no impact, 4 = decisive) of how much payments to parliamentarians for their votes and to officials over the content of decrees affected their business, the measure used in the World Bank's 2006 report. Computed for this map from the 2005 firm-level survey data (World Bank–EBRD; 34 countries in Eastern Europe, Central Asia and Western Europe, plus Turkey and South Korea). Serbia and Montenegro were surveyed together. Old, so weighted low.

colourings.label: Measure: Firms hit by bought votes and decrees, 2002
colourings.note: The same two questions in the 2002 round: firms' average rating (0 = no impact, 4 = decisive) of how much payments to parliamentarians for their votes and to officials over the content of decrees affected their business. Computed for this map from the 2002 firm-level survey data (World Bank–EBRD; 27 countries in Eastern Europe, Central Asia and Turkey). Serbia and Montenegro were surveyed together. Old, so weighted low.

colourings.label: Measure: Firms hit by bought laws, 1999
colourings.note: Business survey across 22 post-Soviet and Eastern European economies. Old, so weighted low by default.
